stage1/problem/A2/v0:
Problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones loaded with expert pixel masks, and uses them both to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses) and to fill the memory bank. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images made from the K normal supports alone — lesion-like patches cut from other normal images of the same modality, intensity-perturbed and Poisson-blended into the support, with the pasted region as the free mask — and how much of the few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of real-abnormal MVFA does this normal-only variant keep on each BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}? A memory-bank-only variant (no fine-tuning on target data) is reported as the lower reference.

Rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, the most expensive annotation in medical imaging, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images and masks contribute. Several related methods show that synthetic anomalies can stand in for real ones when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed's anomaly blending [53], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], LesionPaste [32]), and [55] shows that selecting informative synthetic images matters; but none of them measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter, on the same support set, under an unseen-modality protocol. The question isolates one component — the abnormal half of MVFA's few-shot support set — keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, and needs only image operations on data that BMAD already provides, so it is feasible on one GPU; its answer tells a hospital whether MVFA's few-shot mode can be used before any abnormal case has been annotated.
stage1/problem/B2/v0:
Problem: MVFA's image-level anomaly score is formed by different pooling rules in different places: the paper's image-level loss (Eq. 3) uses the maximum over the anomaly map, the released code trains the detection adapters with a mean-pooled map, and at inference the image score on datasets with masks is the maximum of the fused pixel map while on datasets without masks it is the mean-pooled detection score. Which image-level pooling of the fused anomaly map — maximum, mean, or top-k mean with k as a fraction of the image area in {0.1%, 1%, 5%} — gives the best and most stable few-shot and zero-shot image-level AUROC on each BMAD dataset, and how sensitive is each rule to isolated false-positive pixels, measured by the drop in image-level AUROC when a single high-scoring spurious patch is injected into the maps of normal test images? Training stays as in the released code; only the inference-time pooling changes, and the same rule is applied to all six datasets.

Rationale: L38 and C3 show that one spurious patch can decide an image's label and that the paper and the code disagree on pooling, while L30 shows that the scoring pipeline differs between datasets, so the reported detection numbers cannot be attributed to the method as described. The related literature varies the scoring head but does not isolate pooling for medical CLIP adapters: PatchCore [15] and WinCLIP [12] use maxima, HeadCLIP [17] and LaRP-CLIP [57] add joint or prototype image scores, and CANOR [30] argues that uniform max or mean aggregation of per-class scores ignores how findings combine in chest X-rays. Medical anomalies range from tiny lesions (BrainMRI, LiverCT) to diffuse changes (ChestXray, HIS), so the best pooling rule plausibly depends on the modality, which makes the question relevant to generalisation. It is inference-only on retrained checkpoints, needs a few lines in the test scripts, and yields a single documented scoring rule plus a robustness measure that complements AUROC (L8).
